subtype: Approach: relies on a lucky routine on exam day [Action]
passage: On board exam mornings in their Jaipur colony, Madhav's routine never changed. He checked his pencil box for the blue pen with the chewed cap, the one he'd used since Class 8. On the walk to the bus stop, he stopped at the little Hanuman temple on the corner and pressed his palm to the cool stone wall for a moment. His father, Jagdish, walking beside him, never teased. Madhav had tried to explain once: "It doesn't make me pass. It makes my hands stop shaking." The night before, he had done three past papers and gone to bed at ten. Now, with the pen in his pocket and the wall's coolness still on his palm, he got on the bus breathing slowly.

qa.a: Three past papers.

qa.a: It makes him calmer; he says it makes his hands stop shaking, even though he knows it doesn't make him pass.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see his son's ritual?
qa.a: Jagdish seems respectful and understanding, never teasing, because it helps Madhav stay calm.

grounding: A teenager keeps a lucky pen and touches a temple wall before exams to calm down, while still studying, so the ritual supports effort.

subtype: Approach: expects things to work because they should [Pitfall]
passage: Varun had topped his department and spent four years working late in the lab. When the campus interview call came from a big engineering firm, his friend Shankar asked, "Mock interview tonight?" Varun laughed. "I've worked harder than anyone. It'll go fine." He watched a film instead. The next morning, in the interview room in the Pune office, the first question was, "Tell us about a time you disagreed with a teammate." Varun blanked. Then, "Why this company?" He said something vague about growth. Then, "Explain your final project in two minutes for a non-engineer." He took eight and used jargon. The panel thanked him politely. Walking out, he realised hard work had never taught him how to answer these questions.

qa.q: What was the first interview question?
qa.a: "Tell us about a time you disagreed with a teammate."

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he walked out?
qa.a: He felt shaken and deflated, realising his hard work hadn't prepared him for these questions.

qa.q: What other approach could Varun have taken?
qa.a: Accept Shankar's mock interview and practise common questions, so his real effort could come across clearly.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel hearing how it went?
qa.a: Shankar may feel sorry for Varun, and a little frustrated that his offer was brushed off.

grounding: A student assumes his hard work guarantees a good interview and does no preparation, and the specific questions catch him out.

subtype: Approach: separates comforting rituals from the concrete steps that actually matter [Revision]
passage: The first time I sat the chartered accountancy exam, I failed two papers. I'm Jahnavi. Before every paper I had a ritual: a cup of ginger tea, the same playlist, my grandmother's small silver coin in my pocket. My friend Anjali once asked me, "What else do you do to prepare?" I said, "Study, obviously." But honestly, the ritual had become the preparation. I felt ready because I felt calm. After the result, I sat down and separated the two. The tea and coin stayed; they help me breathe. But I added a mock test every Sunday under exam timing, and I asked a senior to mark my answers and tell me exactly what was weak. The second time, I passed all papers. I still carried the coin.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi add every Sunday?
qa.a: A mock test under exam timing.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel before the first attempt, looking back?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt calm and ready, but that calm came from the ritual, not from real practice.

qa.q: What made the second attempt different?
qa.a: The comforting ritual stayed, but mock tests and a senior's feedback did the real preparing.

qa.q: How might Anjali see the change?
qa.a: Anjali would likely feel glad that the question was taken seriously and pleased to see the pass.

grounding: After failing, the protagonist keeps a calming ritual but adds mock tests and feedback, so comfort no longer stands in for preparation.

subtype: Approach: separates comforting rituals from the concrete steps that actually matter [Revision]
passage:
Driving instructor's note: Sharmila, second attempt

Sharmila failed her first driving test in March. Before it, she told me, she sat in her car for ten minutes with her eyes closed, repeating "I can do this," and felt ready. But she had only practised on quiet roads near her house. This time we talked about it. She decided to keep her ten minutes of calm breathing; it clearly helps her. But she also asked for two mock tests on the actual test route, and she asked me to mark every error on a sheet. Her friend Pallavi drove with her on Sundays to practise reversing. Today, before the test, she sat in the car with her eyes closed. Then she drove. She passed with two minor faults.

qa.q: How many minor faults did Sharmila have?

subtype: Approach: puts off an unpleasant task by doing something easy [Pitfall]

Then I noticed my bookshelf was messy. So I tidied it, by colour. Then my pencils were blunt. I sharpened all of them, even the ones I never use. Then I cleaned my eraser with a tissue. My friend Tenzin rang and I told him I was "doing homework." At dinner, Mummy asked, "Done?" The worksheet was still blank. The bookshelf looked amazing. I felt sick because I still had to do it, and now it was late and I was tired.

qa.q: What did Amandeep tidy first?
qa.a: The bookshelf, by colour.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep keep finding other jobs to do?
qa.a: Amandeep was scared of the long division, and easy jobs felt safer than facing it.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The easy jobs replaced the hard one; starting with just the first question before anything else might make it less scary.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel seeing the blank worksheet at dinner?
qa.a: Mummy might feel frustrated but also concerned, noticing her child was avoiding something scary.

grounding: A boy with a hard maths worksheet tidies his bookshelf and sharpens pencils instead, and the feared task stays untouched.

School counsellor's note: Sachin, Class 11

Sachin came in on Monday because his history essay, 2,000 words, is due Friday and he hasn't started. He showed me his phone's screen time: six hours on Sunday. When I asked what happens when he thinks about the essay, he said, "It's so big I feel tiny. I don't even open the file, because then I'll see how empty it is." He said it without looking up. I asked him to name the smallest possible first step. He thought for a while and said, "Just open the file and write the title." Noor, his classmate, will sit with him in the library at lunch tomorrow while he does that. I will check with him on Wednesday.

subtype: Approach: names the fear behind the delay and takes a small step [Revision]
passage: So I'm Kavitha, and this is about the email I didn't send for nine days. I'd missed a data deadline at work, and I needed to tell my manager, Kishore, that the report would be a week late. Every morning I opened a draft and closed it. One night I asked myself, "What am I actually scared of?" And the answer was simple: I was scared he'd think I was careless. That was it. Once I'd named it, it looked smaller. So I wrote four lines: what happened, what I'd done so far, the new date, and "I'm sorry for the delay." I sent it at 11 p.m. before I could change my mind. He replied the next morning: "Thanks for telling me. Let's talk at ten." The relief was enormous.

qa.q: For how many days did Kavitha avoid sending the email?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What did Kavitha realise was the real fear?
qa.a: Kavitha was afraid of criticism, that Kishore would think the work was careless.

qa.q: Which step helped most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the fear, then writing four short, honest lines and sending them straight away, before the fear could grow again.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the email?
qa.a: Kishore seems to appreciate the honesty, replying calmly and offering to talk rather than scold.

grounding: The protagonist names a fear of criticism, sends a short honest message, and the relief is greater than the worry.

subtype: Approach: names the fear behind the delay and takes a small step [Revision]

qa.a: Ankita may feel relieved for her, and perhaps learn that naming a fear can make a hard message easy to send.

grounding: An observer sees a colleague name her fear of criticism, send a short honest message, and feel great relief.
